intro: Thirty five verses, the longest continuous description of the created world in the book, and the psalm said on Rosh Chodesh in most rites. Two features make it a good page to learn on. The first is the participle used as a divine title: whoever wraps, whoever stretches, whoever lays the beams, whoever makes, whoever sends, whoever looks. Six verses in a row can go by without a finite verb. The second is the archaic ending -un, hung on more than a dozen verbs here, which changes no meaning and marks only that this is old poetry. The psalm also refuses to settle on a person, moving from He to You and back, sometimes inside one verse. Its first four words return as the last four before the closing halleluyah, which is the first halleluyah in the book, so the whole tour of the world sits inside one command the speaker gives to himself.

stichs.en: Bless the LORD, my soul.
LORD my God, You are very great;
splendour and majesty You have put on.

verses.summary: The psalm opens by talking to itself: a feminine imperative addressed to nefesh, the speaker's own soul. Then it turns outward and dresses God the way a king is dressed, which is the image the next two verses expand.

stichs.en: wrapped in light like a cloak,
stretching out the heavens like a tent curtain,

verses.summary: Light is the first thing here, as in Genesis, and it is worn rather than made. The sky is a curtain of goat hair, so what is being described is a tent going up.

stichs.en: who lays the beams of His upper chambers in the waters,
who makes clouds His chariot,
who walks on the wings of the wind,

verses.summary: Building vocabulary applied to water and cloud. Beams laid in water carry nothing, which is the point: the upper storey rests on what could not hold it.

stichs.en: who makes His messengers winds,
His ministers blazing fire.

verses.summary: Wind and fire appear here as staff rather than as weather. The line can be read in either direction, and that ambiguity is old; it is taken up below.

stichs.en: He founded the earth on its foundations,
never to be shaken, for ever and ever.

verses.summary: The foundation laid for the earth answers the beams laid in water above it. What is unsupported up there is fixed down here, and the verse says so twice, once by negation and once by a doubled adverb.

stichs.en: The deep, You covered it like a garment;
above the mountains stood the waters.

verses.summary: For one verse the order is reversed, water on top and mountains submerged. The garment word comes back from verse 2, now covering the earth instead of God.

stichs.en: At Your rebuke they fled,
at the sound of Your thunder they hurried away.

verses.summary: Creation told as a rout. The waters are not drained off, they are frightened away, and both verbs carry the archaic -un ending that runs through the whole psalm.

stichs.en: Mountains rise,
valleys sink,
to the place You founded for them.

verses.summary: Who goes up and who goes down is unsettled in the Hebrew, either the terrain emerging or the water running off it. Either way the movement ends at an assigned place.

stichs.en: A boundary You set, which they shall not cross,
they shall not return to cover the earth.

verses.summary: The first legal word in the psalm. Water is not destroyed, it is given a limit and held to it, which makes dry land a standing decision rather than a fact.

stichs.en: who sends springs into the wadis;
between the mountains they go.

verses.summary: The same water returns, now under orders and useful. It runs where the flood was sent away from, in the dry beds between the hills.

stichs.en: They water every beast of the field;
the wild asses quench their thirst.

verses.summary: The first beneficiaries of the water are not people. Four verses go to animals before a human being appears, and the wild ass is the animal that belongs to nobody.

stichs.en: Beside them the birds of the heavens dwell;
from among the foliage they give voice.

verses.summary: Birds are placed by their address, next to the water and inside the branches. The last two words say only that they make a sound, without saying what it means.

stichs.en: who waters the mountains from His upper chambers;
from the fruit of Your works the earth is satisfied.

verses.summary: The upper chambers of verse 3 turn out to have a function, which is rain. Note the switch from His to Your inside one verse; the psalm does this repeatedly and never smooths it out.

stichs.en: who makes grass grow for the cattle,
and plants for the labour of man,
to bring bread out of the earth,

verses.summary: Two kinds of green for two audiences, one grazed and one worked. Bread is described as something the earth is made to bring out, not as something a farmer makes.

stichs.en: and wine that gladdens the heart of a mortal,
to make the face shine with oil,
and bread that sustains a mortal's heart.

verses.summary: Past survival. Bread, wine and oil are the standard triad of the land's produce, and only the first keeps anyone alive; the other two are for gladness and for a face that shines.

stichs.en: The trees of the LORD are satisfied,
the cedars of Lebanon which He planted,

verses.summary: Trees nobody planted and nobody irrigates. Cedars are the biblical measure of what is too large for human management, so they are listed as fed rather than as harvested.

stichs.en: where the birds make their nests;
the stork, the cypresses are her house.

verses.summary: The tree is now described from the bird's side. A cypress is not scenery in this line, it is a house with a named occupant.

stichs.en: The high mountains are for the wild goats,
the crags a refuge for the rock badgers.

verses.summary: Two habitats nobody else wants, high ground and bare rock. The psalm keeps assigning places, and the assignment is itself the provision.

stichs.en: He made the moon for appointed times;
the sun knows its setting.

verses.summary: The moon is given a job and the sun keeps a schedule. Time enters here, and the next four verses run one full night and day through it.

stichs.en: You make darkness and it is night,
in it every beast of the forest creeps about.

verses.summary: Darkness is made, not merely allowed to fall. Night is the shift when the forest animals hold the world, and the psalm does not treat that as a threat.

stichs.en: The young lions roar for prey,
and to seek their food from God.

verses.summary: The roar is classified as a form of asking. The verse turns a predator into a creature waiting on a table it does not set.

stichs.en: The sun rises, they gather themselves in,
and lie down in their dens.

verses.summary: Sunrise closes the animals' shift. Two verbs with the same archaic ending end the night, and the next verse opens the human one.

stichs.en: A man goes out to his work,
and to his labour until evening.

verses.summary: One verse for humanity, the same six words the lions were given. The working day is bounded at both ends, and the boundary named here is evening.

stichs.en: How many are Your works, LORD!
In wisdom You made them all;
the earth is full of Your creatures.

verses.summary: The catalogue breaks off and the psalm exclaims. Wisdom is named as the method, which is as close as this psalm comes to a theory of how the world was made.

stichs.en: This sea, great and broad of hands,
there are creeping things beyond number,
living things small along with great.

verses.summary: The sea is the single largest item in the catalogue and takes thirteen words, a length matched only by the closing verse. Its contents are counted only as uncountable.

stichs.en: There the ships go,
there is Leviathan, whom You formed to play in it.

verses.summary: Cargo traffic and the sea monster share one lane. The last two words are the ones the tradition argued over, because they can put the playing on either side.

stichs.en: All of them look to You,
to give them their food in its time.

verses.summary: The catalogue becomes dependence. Everything listed since verse 10 collapses into one subject, all of them, and one posture, waiting.

stichs.en: You give to them, they gather;
You open Your hand, they are filled with good.

verses.summary: Four verbs in seven words, alternating between the hand that opens and the mouths that fill. Nothing is stored; the giving and the gathering happen in the same breath.

stichs.en: You hide Your face, they are terrified;
You gather in their breath, they expire,
and to their dust they return.

verses.summary: The same grammar delivers death. Hiding the face and taking back the breath are the exact negatives of opening the hand, and the verse ends on the word from Genesis 3, dust.

stichs.en: You send Your breath, they are created,
and You renew the face of the ground.

verses.summary: One noun covers wind, breath and spirit, so the wind of verse 4 turns out to be what animates the animals of verse 29. Renewal is described as a face changing, not as a repair.

stichs.en: May the glory of the LORD last for ever;
may the LORD rejoice in His works.

verses.summary: The first request in the psalm, after thirty verses of pure description. What it asks for is that the maker go on enjoying what was made.

stichs.en: who looks at the earth and it trembles,
touches the mountains and they smoke.

verses.summary: The earth that could not be shaken in verse 5 shakes under a glance. The verse follows the request on purpose: what was asked for is not a mild thing.

stichs.en: I will sing to the LORD while I live,
I will make music to my God while I still am.

verses.summary: The speaker returns, absent since verse 1. Two verbs of singing, each with a time limit attached, and the limit is one human lifetime.

stichs.en: May my musing be sweet to Him;
as for me, I will rejoice in the LORD.

verses.summary: What is offered is the speech itself, and it is offered in the hope of being accepted. Sweet here is the vocabulary of an offering that is received.

stichs.en: May sinners be finished from the earth,
and the wicked be no more.
Bless the LORD, my soul.
Halleluyah.

verses.summary: The one harsh line in the psalm, and the tradition read it against itself. Then the opening returns word for word, and the first halleluyah in the book closes the whole thing.

pardes.body: A tour of the world in the order of Genesis 1, with one command wrapped around it. Verses 1 to 4 dress God and pitch the sky; 5 to 9 set the earth and push the water back behind a boundary; 10 to 18 let the same water out again and follow it to everything that drinks it; 19 to 23 run a night and a day; 24 stops to exclaim; 25 and 26 handle the sea; 27 to 30 turn the catalogue into dependence, where food, breath and death all come from the same hand; 31 to 35 respond. The frame is exact: {{1.0}} and {{1.1}} return as {{35.7}} and {{35.8}}, so everything between is what the soul is being told to bless. Two habits are worth watching while reading. The psalm names participles rather than actions, so God is identified by what He is always doing, and it slides between He and You without warning, as at verse 13, where the upper chambers are His and the works in the same verse are Yours.

Verse 4 is ambiguous in the Hebrew and the ambiguity is not resolvable from word order alone: {{4.0}} with {{4.1}} and {{4.2}} can mean who makes winds His messengers, or who makes His messengers into winds. The first keeps the verse in the weather of verses 2 and 3, the second makes it a line about angels, and both readings are old. Verse 8 has the same problem with subjects: {{8.0}} and {{8.2}} can describe mountains rising and valleys sinking as the land emerges, or the water of verse 7 running up and down the terrain as it flees. In {{15.6}} the prefix is the ambiguous mem, so the face shines with oil or shines more than oil. {{25.3}} with {{25.4}} is literally broad of hands, an idiom for wide reaching, and {{11.4}} is literally to break, used here of breaking a thirst. Then there is the ending -un on more than a dozen verbs, from {{7.2}} to {{30.2}}: it adds nothing to the meaning and is one of the clearest markers in the book that a text is deliberately archaic.

The Talmud at Berakhot 10a reports the best known reading of the last verse. Rabbi Meir prayed for the death of the troublemakers in his neighbourhood, and Beruriah, his wife, pointed at {{35.1}}: the consonants say chata'im, which can be read as sins rather than as sinners, and the next clause then follows on its own, because once sins are finished the wicked are no more. Rabbi Meir prayed for their repentance instead. On {{26.6}} the Talmud at Avodah Zarah 3b reads the playing as God's own, and says He spends part of each day playing with Leviathan, which turns the verse from a note on sea life into a statement that creation includes leisure. The custom of saying this psalm on Rosh Chodesh is usually explained from two lines inside it, {{19.1}}, the moon made for appointed times, and {{30.3}}, the renewal of the face of the ground, so the monthly renewal of the moon and the renewal of the world are read as one subject.

The garment of {{2.0}} and {{2.1}} is the standard mystical image for a light that hides what it reveals: what can be seen of God is exactly the covering, and the world is the outside of the garment. The midrashic tradition on the first day of creation answers the question of where that light came from by pointing at this verse. The deeper move is in verses 29 and 30, which use one word, ruach, for wind, breath and spirit, and describe creatures as created when it is sent and expiring when it is gathered back. Read that way the psalm is not about an event but about a continuous supply: nothing here holds itself in existence for a moment, and the difference between a living animal and dust is which direction the breath is moving. {{26.6}} belongs to the same reading. A world made for play is a world not made from need, which is the usual mystical answer to why anything was created at all.
